summary: Walter L. Criley, writing on behalf of the Tennessee Department of Conservation's Division of Planning & Development, offers conditional support for ORV regulation, raising specific concerns about environmental disturbances from designated ORV areas, the difficulty of controlling underage vehicle operators, and the risk that opening some areas will lead users to assume all public lands are open. He concludes by welcoming the Department of the Interior's recognition of the problems ORVs create, but insists that the resulting regulations must be carefully analyzed and strictly enforced to protect the integrity of public lands.

statement.text:
Dear Mr. Wellborn:
We have reviewed the above captioned statement and offer the following comments:
a. (Page 6) Under the operating criteria subsection, permits may be issued for the operation of Off-Road Vehicles on areas designated for their use for organized races. Criteria for the selection of these areas should carefully weigh the resulting environmental disturbances to the area. Also relating to this subsection, the operation of motorized vehicles (especially motorcycles and minibikes) by persons under legal licensing age will be difficult to control.
b. (Page 12) The second paragraph on this page states that ORV's provide safe and convenient transportation to portions of the public lands not otherwise accessible to the benefit of society. The inaccessibility of many public lands is the very factor that attracts many people to these areas. Cheapening the quality of a person's visit by making all areas easily accessible (along with the resultant environmental disturbances inherent to ORV's) will accelerate the already rapidly diminishing areas suitable for a quality natural experience.
c. (Page 14) ORV use in camping and picnicking areas will tend to push wildlife in these areas into more remote sections. The loss of these animals will detract from the quality of a recreational visit.
d. (Page 16) In the long run, ORV use will result in more forest fires being started than it will aid in the prevention of these fires.

e. (Page 19) Care should be taken to insure that, with the opening of certain areas to ORV use, the user does not come to think that all areas of the public lands are open to the use of his vehicle.
146
f. (Page 26) On this page a paragraph states: "Within designated ORV areas some irreversible or irretrievable impacts upon land forms, wildlife and their habitat, and historical and archeological sites may occur despite the utmost of precautions." Again careful attention should be focused upon the criteria of areas zoned for ORV use to hold their cultural and environmental impact to a minimum.
It seems that any recreational form that becomes popular and economical will be welcomed to the public lands. Accepting this fact leads one to wonder, should the average citizen find himself capable of purchasing bulldozers and army surplus tanks, will he be allowed access with these vehicles to the public lands?
It is good to see that the Department of the Interior recognizes the problem that ORV's create and is trying to regulate their use. These regulations should be carefully analyzed and strictly enforced to insure the perpetuation and undiminished integrity of our public lands.
Sincerely,
Walter L. Criley
